solvers.working: Work = F·d, a dot product, so it is a scalar. Momentum = mv is a vector. Electric current has a direction along the conductor but does not obey vector addition (the parallelogram law), so it is treated as a scalar. Pressure = force per unit area, acting equally in all directions, so it is a scalar.
solvers.value: Work, electric current and pressure are scalars
solvers.note: Electric current is a standard textbook example of a scalar, even though it is drawn with a direction, because it does not follow vector addition. Pressure is also a scalar even though it is defined using force.

solvers.working: Work W = F·d is a dot product, so it is a scalar. Momentum p = mv has direction and adds as a vector, so it is a vector. Electric current has a sense of flow but does not obey vector addition (currents at a junction add algebraically), so it is a scalar. Pressure is normal force per unit area, it acts equally in all directions at a point and has no specific direction, so it is a scalar.

(C) 1 s

before.solution_html: Time to reach the top = u/g = 2 s. Time to come back = 2 s. Total time = 4 s.

after.question_html:
A ball is thrown vertically upward with a speed of 20 m/s (g = 10 m/s2). After how long does it return to the thrower's hand?
(A) 2 s
(B) 4 s
(C) 1 s
(D) 8 s
after.solution_html: Time to reach the top = u/g = 2 s. Time to come back = 2 s. Total time = 4 s.

solvers.working:
Take upward as positive, with the ball returning to the same height as the hand.
Displacement is zero: 0 = ut - (1/2)gt^2
So t = 2u/g = 2(20)/10 = 4 s.
Check: time to the top is u/g = 2 s, and the fall takes the same 2 s, so the total is 4 s.

For a ball thrown vertically upward, the time of flight back to the launch point is T = 2u/g.
Substituting u = 20 m/s and g = 10 m/s^2: T = 2(20)/10 = 4 s.
Check: the time to reach the top is u/g = 2 s, and the fall back takes the same 2 s, giving 4 s in total.

before.question_html:
A uniform rod of length L, pivoted at one end, is released from rest in the horizontal position. Its angular speed when it becomes vertical is
(A) √(3g/L)
(B) √(g/L)
(C) √(2g/L)
(D) √(6g/L)
before.solution_html: Loss in potential energy = M g L/2 = (1/2) I ω2 with I = M L2/3. So ω = √(3g/L).

after.question_html:
A uniform rod of length L, pivoted at one end, is released from rest in the horizontal position. Its angular speed when it becomes vertical is
(A) √(3g/L)
(B) √(g/L)
(C) √(2g/L)
(D) √(6g/L)
after.solution_html: Loss in potential energy = M g L/2 = (1/2) I ω2 with I = M L2/3. So ω = √(3g/L).

solvers.working:
Energy conservation: the centre of mass falls by L/2, so loss in PE = mgL/2.
Rotational KE = (1/2) I ω² with I = mL²/3 about the pivot, so KE = mL²ω²/6.
Set mgL/2 = mL²ω²/6, which gives ω² = 3g/L.
Therefore ω = √(3g/L).

The rod's centre of mass falls by L/2 as it swings from horizontal to vertical, so it loses PE = mgL/2.
About the pivot, I = mL²/3, so KE = (1/2)(mL²/3)ω².
Energy conservation: (1/2)(mL²/3)ω² = mgL/2.
This gives ω² = 3g/L, so ω = √(3g/L).

vote.explanation: Key, solution and solvers all give A.
